input.summary: The paper claim asserts that adding 20 ms of one-way delay under fixed emulated bottleneck conditions changes TCP flow completion time. The user context notes a LEO optical-link terminal with no hardware, orbital trace, or physical access. Because the claim is purely about emulated network conditions (delay + bottleneck → FCT change), it is directly testable in the emulated-netem-v1 runner without any real hardware. The proposed pilot compares two delay conditions (0 ms vs. 20 ms one-way client delay) across three standard TCP congestion control algorithms (cubic, bbr, reno) and two representative file sizes, under a fixed bottleneck rate and buffer, with multiple replications to characterize FCT distributions. The LEO/optical-link context motivates the 20 ms delay value (plausible LEO one-way propagation) but the experiment itself is fully synthetic. Key open questions concern the intended bottleneck rate, buffer size, and whether the claim is directional (delay increases FCT) or merely asserts a non-zero difference.
questions: What bottleneck link rate (Mbit/s) and buffer size (kbytes) does the paper specify or imply for the fixed emulated bottleneck conditions?
Is the claim directional — i.e., does the paper assert that 20 ms delay *increases* FCT relative to 0 ms delay, or only that FCT *changes* (could be either direction depending on CCA)?
Which TCP congestion control algorithm(s) does the paper evaluate under these conditions (e.g., CUBIC, BBR, Reno), and what file/transfer sizes are used?
